topic: cleaning and regulating an inherited longcase clock

provenance.author: glowny-en-d
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is clock arithmetic (gear turns, beats, rating nut turns, winding turns) with closed task questions, base is a dialogue about cleaning and regulating a gaining longcase clock. Grounded external referent: the train of wheels, introduced in turn 0 (it is dusty, gets cleaned and turned by hand) and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion.

a: Here is the service sheet for one longcase clock, and the counts need working through in order.
The great wheel carries ninety-six teeth and drives a pinion of eight leaves.
The centre wheel carries sixty-four teeth and drives a second pinion of eight.
The pendulum beats once every second, hour after hour, when the clock runs true.
How many turns does the pinion of eight make for one turn of the great wheel?
base: My grandmother's longcase clock has started gaining time badly since it was moved into the hall.
It gains several minutes every week now, and the strike has gone ragged as well.
Behind the dial the train of wheels looks dusty, and the oil has turned dark and gummy.
The case and dial are lovely, and I want to care for the works myself.
Where should a careful beginner start with a clock that is running fast and dirty?

a: One full turn of the great wheel turns the pinion of eight around twelve times over.
The centre wheel in turn spins its own pinion eight times for every revolution.
A pendulum beating once a second makes three thousand six hundred beats in an hour.
Across a full day of running that comes to eighty-six thousand four hundred beats in total.
Does the daily beat count match the figure printed on the service sheet?
base: Start by letting the weights down gently and lifting the hood clear of the case.
Take the pendulum off its crutch before anything else, because a swinging bob punishes careless hands.
Look at each pivot hole in the plates for the black paste of old oil and brass dust.
Follow the train wheel by wheel with a lamp, and note every tooth that looks worn.
Is the clock striking the wrong count, or striking at the wrong minute?

a: Now take the gaining rate, because the sheet records ninety seconds gained every day.
One full turn of the rating nut changes the rate by thirty seconds a day.
Turns of the nut can only be counted in halves on this clock.
State the direction too, since a gaining clock needs the bob let down.
How many turns of the nut cancel a gain of ninety seconds a day?
base: The strike counts correctly but lands three or four minutes after the hour hand.
Dust lies along the train so thick that the lamp shows grey ridges on every wheel.
Two pivot holes in the front plate look stretched into little ovals rather than circles.
The oil at every hole has dried to the black paste you described.
Can I clean the works without pulling the plates apart on my first attempt?

a: Ninety seconds divided by thirty seconds a turn calls for three full turns of the nut.
Three turns can be counted in halves, so the setting is six half turns down.
The bob drops slightly with each half turn, slowing the swing by a small step.
After the turns the expected rate sits at zero seconds gained or lost.
Is three turns down the figure that goes into the service record?
base: A first cleaning can be done with the movement whole, though a full strip does it better.
Brush every wheel with a dry stiff brush, then follow with sticks of pegwood in the holes.
Turn the train slowly by hand afterwards and listen for any grating from the pivots.
The stretched oval holes will need a clockmaker's bushing before another winter passes.
Do the worn holes sit on the going side, or over on the striking side?

a: One correction before the record is written, because the rate was measured again overnight.
The clock gains one hundred twenty seconds a day, not the ninety on the sheet.
Recalculate the turns of the nut at the same thirty seconds for every turn.
Report the setting in half turns as well, the way this clock is counted.
What does the correction become at one hundred twenty seconds a day?
base: The worn holes both sit on the going side, one at the centre wheel pivot.
I must correct something I said earlier, because I timed the clock properly overnight.
It gains two minutes a day, not several minutes a week as I first guessed.
Turning the train by hand feels smooth now that the pegwood has done its work.
Does a gain that size point to something worse than dust and old oil?

a: One hundred twenty seconds at thirty seconds a turn calls for four full turns down.
Counted in halves, the setting is eight half turns down on the rating nut.
The new figure replaces the six half turns entered from the earlier rate.
After the setting the expected daily error returns to zero on the sheet.
Is eight half turns the figure that now stands in the service record?
base: A gain of two minutes a day is nearly always the pendulum, not the wheels.
Check whether the bob has crept up the rod, because a shorter swing runs fast.
The rating nut under the bob lets you lower it a little at a time.
Lower the bob by small, even steps, timing the clock against the radio each day.
Is the pendulum rod wood or metal, since the two drift differently with the seasons?

a: Now count the winding, because the weights drop the length of the case each week.
The going weight falls sixty inches in seven days of steady running.
The barrel takes up five inches of line with every turn of the key.
Both weights are wound fully home on the same morning each week.
How many key turns lift the going weight after its full weekly drop?
base: The rod is wood with a brass cap, and the bob slides stiffly but evenly.
I lowered the bob two small steps and the gain fell to about forty seconds.
The hall is cooler than the old room, which may explain some of the change.
The strike still lands late, though the hours count correctly every time.
How do I bring the strike back to the minute without upsetting the rate?

a: Sixty inches at five inches a turn calls for twelve turns of the key.
The striking weight takes the same twelve turns because its weekly drop is the same sixty inches.
Twenty-four turns in all bring both weights fully home on the winding morning.
At one winding a week the clock takes fifty-two windings across a full year.
Does the twelve turn figure agree with the note on the case door?
base: The strike is set by the minute hand's position, not by anything inside the count.
Move the minute hand gently forward until the strike falls, then set it to that minute.
Never wind the hands backwards through the strike, because that is how levers get bent.
If the warning runs early or late by the same margin, the hand itself is loose.
Does the minute hand sit tight on its post, or can you wiggle it?

a: Now close the sheet with the service summary in the order the work was done.
Step one is the cleaning, step two the rating, and step three the winding count.
The rating stands at eight half turns down from the setting found on arrival.
The winding stands at twelve key turns for each weight on winding morning.
The summary line reads cleaned, rated and counted, with the date beside it.
base: The minute hand had worked loose, and tightening its little pin cured the late strike.
The clock has run two days now at under ten seconds of gain a day.
I will keep lowering the bob by half steps until the gain disappears.
The hall sounds right again with the tick and the hour strike back in step.
My grandmother would be pleased to hear it keeping honest time in my house.

a: The summary closes with the three steps entered in their working order on the sheet.
The cleaning entry carries the pegwood note and the two worn holes for the record.
The rating entry carries eight half turns down and the zero expected error.
The winding entry carries twelve turns a weight and fifty-two windings a year.
The sheet is complete from first count to final entry with nothing left open.
base: Half steps on the nut are exactly right, and a week between changes is even better.
Write the date and the size of every change on a card kept inside the case.
Book the bushing work for the worn holes before the winter damp arrives.
A clean, rated clock with sound pivots should run for years between services.
Old clocks reward patience, and this one clearly has plenty of care coming its way.
